title: Review: Blood clotting and blood cells; Statistical tests; Experimental design and variables
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Edexcel A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: PR01a#t3 term and clue written for the game; PR01a#t4 term and clue written for the game; PR03b#t1 term and clue written for the game; PR03b#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: IM10#N.5, PR01a#N.10, PR03a#N.3, PR03b#N.9, IM10#N.3, PR01a#N.8, PR03a#N.11, PR03b#N.7, IM10#N.7, PR01a#N.6, PR01a#N.2a. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Positive control
items.clue: Set-up in which an effect is known to occur, showing the method can detect one.

items.label: Null hypothesis
items.clue: States that the factor being changed has no effect, or that there is no difference.

items.label: Student's t-test
items.clue: Used to compare two means of continuous data that are roughly normally distributed.

items.label: Critical value
items.clue: Number at p = 0.05 that t must equal or exceed for the difference to be significant.

questions.stem: Fibrinogen circulates in the plasma of healthy people all the time, yet clots form only where a blood vessel has been damaged. Which statement best explains this?

options.text: Fibrinogen is converted to fibrin only when it is exposed to the air at an open wound, so a clot cannot form inside a vessel that is intact.
Fibrin is already present in the plasma, but its threads only become tangled into a mesh where the flow of blood is disturbed by damage.
The cascade has so many steps that it is too slow to finish unless the blood is held still against the wall of a damaged vessel.
Thrombin, the enzyme that converts fibrinogen to fibrin, is produced by a cascade that starts only when platelets release clotting factors at a site of damage.

questions.stem: Ecologists want to test the hypothesis that two limpet species compete for algae on a shore. Which approach tests the hypothesis by experiment rather than by observation?

options.text: Removing one limpet species from marked plots and recording the growth of the other over a year.
Recording the abundance of both limpet species in quadrats placed at random positions along the shore.
Measuring the shell sizes of both limpet species in laboratory tanks of seawater collected from the shore.
Applying a chi-squared test to records of where each species occurred in past shore surveys.

questions.stem: A student measures the lengths of 20 leaves from plants growing in the sun and 20 from plants growing in the shade. She wants to know whether mean leaf length differs between the two. Which statistical test should she use?

options.text: Chi-squared, because she is comparing two groups of plants.
Student's t-test, because she is comparing the means of two sets of continuous data.
A correlation coefficient, because she wants to know whether light is related to leaf length.
No test is needed: if the two means differ, the difference is real.

questions.explanation: Two groups, one measured variable, a difference in means: that is what the t-test is for.

questions.stem: A student counts the heart rate of Daphnia in pond water (control) and in a caffeine solution, 10 Daphnia in each. - Control: mean 212 beats per minute, SD 18. - Caffeine: mean 231 beats per minute, SD 20. Critical values of t at p = 0.05: 9 degrees of freedom, 2.26; 18, 2.10; 20, 2.09. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: t = 9.75, far above 2.10, so the difference is highly significant.
t = 2.23, above 2.10 for 18 degrees of freedom, so reject the null hypothesis.
t = 2.23, below 2.26 for 9 degrees of freedom, so accept the null hypothesis.
t = 2.23, above 2.10, which proves caffeine raises the heart rate of every Daphnia.

questions.stem: Fibrinogen circulates in the blood all the time. Why does a clot form at a cut, but not throughout the blood vessels?

options.text: Thrombin, which converts fibrinogen to fibrin, is made only where clotting factors are released.
Fibrinogen turns into fibrin only when the blood at a cut is exposed to the air.
Fibrin threads are in the blood all the time, but they tangle together only where blood flow slows at a cut.
Platelets stick together into a plug at the cut, and this plug alone is the clot, with no plasma proteins needed.

questions.explanation: The cascade starts only at the wound, so thrombin, and so fibrin, forms only there. Elsewhere fibrinogen stays soluble.

questions.stem: A filter-paper disc soaked in catalase solution sinks in hydrogen peroxide and rises when enough oxygen has formed on it. In 1% hydrogen peroxide the disc took 50 s to rise; in 2% it took 20 s. Which statement about the reaction rate is correct?

options.text: Rate is proportional to 1/time, so the rate at 2% (0.05 s⁻¹) is 2.5 times the rate at 1% (0.02 s⁻¹).
The rate at 1% is 50 and at 2% is 20, so the rate fell when the concentration was doubled.
Doubling the concentration doubles the rate, so the rate at 2% is 0.04 s⁻¹, twice that at 1%.
The rate cannot be found, because the volume of oxygen produced was not measured in either trial.

questions.stem: A 1999 study found that children who had slept with a light on before the age of two were more likely to become short-sighted later. Later studies found that short-sighted parents were more likely to leave a light on at night, and short sight is partly inherited. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: Night-time lighting causes short sight, because the 1999 correlation was found in a large group of children.
The correlation can be explained by parents' short sight, which is linked to both variables.
The 1999 correlation must have been a mistake: the children with night lights were not really more short-sighted.
The later studies prove that light at night has no effect on the eye at all.

questions.stem: For 10 quadrats, a student ranks the density of a moss and the soil moisture content, and finds Σd² = 60. The critical value of rₛ for n = 10 at p = 0.05 is 0.648. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: rₛ = 0.64, which is below 0.648, so there is no significant correlation.
rₛ = 0.36, a weak positive correlation that is not significant.
rₛ = 0.64, a positive value, so there is a significant positive correlation.
rₛ = 0.64, which is greater than 0.05, so the correlation is significant.

questions.explanation: rₛ = 1 − (6 × 60) ÷ (10 × 99) = 1 − 360 ÷ 990 = 0.64. Just below the critical value: the correlation could be due to chance.

questions.stem: The drug warfarin blocks the use of vitamin K in the liver. The liver needs vitamin K to make prothrombin. What happens to the blood of a person taking warfarin?

options.text: It clots more slowly, because without vitamin K platelets cannot stick to form a plug.
It clots normally, because platelets alone form the clot that seals a cut.
It clots normally, because fibrin threads are already present in the plasma.
It clots more slowly, because less prothrombin means less thrombin is made.

questions.explanation: Less thrombin converts less fibrinogen to fibrin, so the mesh forms more slowly. Warfarin is used to prevent unwanted clots.

questions.stem: A student plans to test whether the number of double bonds in a fatty acid affects its melting point, using fatty acids with 0, 1, 2 and 3 double bonds that all have the same chain length. Which statement is an appropriate null hypothesis for this investigation?

options.text: Fatty acids with more double bonds will melt at lower temperatures than those with fewer.
Fatty acids with more double bonds will melt at higher temperatures than those with fewer.
The number of double bonds in a fatty acid has no effect on its melting point.
None of the fatty acids will melt at any of the temperatures used in the investigation.

questions.stem: A student places a lamp at different distances from a beaker of pondweed in sodium hydrogencarbonate solution kept at 25 °C, and counts the bubbles of gas released per minute at each distance. Which correctly identifies the variables?

options.text: Independent: lamp distance; dependent: bubbles per minute
Independent: bubbles per minute; dependent: distance of lamp
Controlled variable: lamp distance; dependent: bubbles per minute
Independent: temperature of 25 °C; dependent: bubbles per minute

questions.explanation: The lamp distance is what the student deliberately changes (it sets the light intensity), so it is the independent variable; the bubble count is measured to find the effect, so it is the dependent variable. Temperature and hydrogencarbonate concentration are controlled variables.
